summary: Gives three distribution lists for network documents: list A for sites sending their own documents, and lists B and C for the Network Information Center to send copies to other participants. It replaces RFC 95 and RFC 155 and was replaced by RFC 211.

eli5.summary: An updated address list for mailing paper notes to people who need them. There are three lists for different jobs.

questions: what were the arpanet mailing lists a b and c
subtitle: Distribution mailing lists for early ARPANET documents.

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET participants needed a way to receive copies of Request for Comments (RFCs) and other network documents, but the distribution system was not clearly specified.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 168 provides three mailing lists: List A for site liaisons receiving initial distribution, List B for network participants, and List C for station agents handling distribution for their sites, all using postal mail.
tldr.outcome: Network documentation could be reliably distributed via mail to the correct recipients at each ARPANET site, replacing the prior ad-hoc system.

today: RFC 168 is a historic document. It was obsoleted by RFC 211, which provided updated mailing lists. Today, RFCs are distributed electronically via the RFC Editor website, and IANA maintains contact information. This RFC is of historical interest only.

sections.title: The ARPANET Mailing System
sections.content:
RFC 168, published in May 1971, specified how Request for Comments and other network documents should be distributed among ARPANET nodes. At that time, ARPANET was a small research network connecting about 20 computers at universities and research institutes. Documents were distributed on paper via postal mail.

RFC 168 supersedes RFC 95 and RFC 155, showing that the mailing lists required periodic updates as sites joined and participants changed.
sections.eli5: In 1971, RFCs were printed on paper and mailed to people. This RFC said who to mail them to at each site.

sections.title: Three Distribution Lists
sections.content:
List A (Initial Distribution) contains Network Liaisons and key contacts who should receive all RFCs and formal documents from the Network Information Center. This list includes representatives from major nodes such as AMES, MIT, CMU, Stanford, UCLA, UCSB, and others.

List B (General Distribution from NIC) includes broader participants who should receive formal documents but not necessarily every RFC. Examples include EDUCOM, regional networks, and university computer centers.

List C (Station Agents) names the administrative staff at each site responsible for receiving and distributing documents locally within their organization.
sections.eli5: List A: important people who need everything. List B: other sites that should get formal documents. List C: the people at each site who handle the paperwork.

sections.title: Historical Impact
sections.content: RFC 168 was one of the first administrative documents, showing how early ARPANET participants organized themselves. Its existence demonstrates that the network had to solve practical distribution problems even in 1971. The mailing lists themselves are now historical—these specific researchers and institutions were the foundation of what became the modern Internet, though nearly all the addresses in RFC 168 are no longer active.
sections.eli5: This RFC shows how scientists in 1971 coordinated sharing ideas on an experimental network. It's a snapshot of early computing history.
